newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mixed as stocks bounce.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mixed as stocks bounce.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mixed Tuesday, in a low volume sequel to Monday's sell off, despite further gains in U.S. stocks and bonds after interest rates were left unchanged at the U.S. Federal Reserve's open market committee meeting (FOMC).
"Gold saw a little bounce back from yesterday's sell off, but it was largely a featureless day, despite the volatility in stocks and bonds," FIMAT New York broker John Tyree said.
COMEX December gold ended up $1.80 an ounce at $326.50, recovering some of Monday's $4.80 loss.
Estimated COMEX gold volume was only 17,000 lots.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $323.00/50, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $323.45 and the New York close Monday around $321.10/60 an ounce.

After sliding to new 12-year lows around $315 in early July, spot gold has recovered some ground, but has constantly run into resistance just below $330 an ounce, leading some analysts to believe a central bank forward sale program is underway again.

Implied gold lease rates eased Tuesday to 2.44 pct for one month from 2.75 pct Monday, though 12 month rates were little changed around 2.35 pct, leaving the forward lease curve still inverted, and near its highest levels since January when the Dutch central bank sold 300 tonnes of gold.

The high and inverted gold forward lease rate curve may reflect borrowing by bullion banks to finance a central bank forward sale program, traders said, but officals at the Dutch central bank would make no comment early Tuesday.
"Gold is very, very tight in the London market at present," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a report.
"There is very heavy borrowing going on which could represent producer selling or it could represent a bullion house borrowing in gold ahead of selling it out for a central bank," he said.
"Or it could represent a really tight physical supply shortage in the near term given the strong physical offtake that we have seen in recent months in Asia, India and the Middle East."
COMEX September silver ended up 1.0 cent at $4.512 an ounce, after giving back some of last week's gains Monday.
Last week September silver saw its highest level since early July.

Open interest in September silver fell 2,774 lots to 45,439 contracts or 227,195,000 ounces Monday, but remains higher than COMEX warehouse silver stocks which fell 152,949 ounces Monday to 165,243,018 ounces.
COMEX warehouse silver stocks are about 20 million ounces lower than at the end of June, and almost 38 million ounces lower than at the start of 1997.
"The discrepancy between open interest and warehouse stocks could lend support to silver prices at the end of August when the contract is deliverable," CPM Group analyst Ted Kemp said.
First notice day for September silver is on August 29.
"Similarly, working stocks of silver in Bombay are currently around 160,754 ounces and some refiners have been unable to meet fabriators requirements," Kempf said.

Moreover, strong growth in amateur photography will push photographic demand for silver to 233 million ounces this year, up three percent over the 1996 level, according to silver analyst Peter Krause in a mid-year industry outlook released Tuesday by the Silver Institute.
However, NYMEX October platinum ended down $8.40 at $408.00 an ounce Tuesday, its lowest level since late July, while NYMEX September palladium ended down the $6.00 daily limit at $197.50.
Talk of spot market platinum group metal (PGM) sales by both Russian and Swiss dealers overnight, plus a break of the $200.00 level in September palladium set off stop orders on NYMEX, traders said.
Lease rates for platinum group metals (PGMs) were little changed early Tuesday, after easing Monday to around 15 pct for one month platinum and 50 pct for one month palladium.
But "demand for these two metals has more than doubled since the mid-1980s," CPM Group's Kempf noted.
"Supply has kept pace with this growth in demand until 1997, but there are serious questions about the outlook for the next few years."
